lessons.title: Building an induction proof
lessons.summary: Connect a verified starting case to every later integer, rather than extrapolating a pattern.
lessons.objective: Prove finite-sum identities by a valid base case, hypothesis and forward implication.
lessons.before: Review finite sums and polynomial factorisation. You need to distinguish an identity, a conjecture and a conditional statement.
lessons.ideas:
What must travel from one integer to the next?

Let P(n) be a precise statement for integers \(n\ge n_0\). Checking P at several values is evidence for a conjecture, not a proof for infinitely many values. Induction needs two logically separate facts:

  1. \(P(n_{0})\) is true by a direct calculation.
  2. For an arbitrary integer \(k\ge n_0\), if P(k) is true, then P(k+1) is true.

The second fact is a conditional implication: temporarily use P(k), never P(k+1). The starting case then triggers every successive implication. Without a starting case, a perfectly valid implication might never begin.

Name the target before doing the algebra

For \(S_n=\sum_{r=a}^{n}t_r\), define P(n) as \(S_n=F(n)\), with \(n\ge a\). At n=a the sum has one term. At the next stage, only the new upper term is added:

\[S_{k+1}=S_k+t_{k+1}=F(k)+t_{k+1}.\]

Use algebra to reach F(k+1). You may write F(k+1) separately as your target, but cannot assume it equals the new sum. A useful independent check is \(F(k+1)-F(k)=t_{k+1}\), together with the correct starting value.

Scope and conclusion

State that \(P(n_{0})\) and the implication prove P(n) for every integer \(n\ge n_{0}\). A start at 3 proves nothing about 1 or 2. A step of two requires a base in each parity class you intend to cover, or a conclusion restricted to one parity. Finite examples can disprove a statement: one counterexample is enough.
lessons.method:
1. State P(n) and its integer domain.
  2. Evaluate both sides at the actual starting index.
  3. Assume P(k) for one arbitrary admissible k.
  4. Add the new term and simplify to the exact k+1 target.
  5. Conclude with the base case, implication and full domain.
mistakes: Several successful substitutions do not establish an infinite claim.
Do not assume the target P(k+1) in your working.
The added term is t(k+1), not t(k).
A sum starting at a has one term when n=a.

examples.title: 1 · A starting index that is not 1
examples.question: Prove \(\sum_{r=3}^{n}(2r+1)=(n+1)^2-9\) for every integer \(n\ge 3\).
examples.solution:
Let P(n) be this identity. At n=3 the left side is 7 and the right side is 16−9=7. Assume P(k) for an arbitrary \(k\ge 3\). Then

\[\sum_{r=3}^{k+1}(2r+1)=(k+1)^2-9+2k+3=(k+2)^2-9.\]

This is P(k+1). The verified base and implication prove the identity for all integers \(n\ge 3\).

examples.title: 2 · Keep the new term visible
examples.question: Prove \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}r(2r+3)=n(n+1)(4n+11)/6\), \(n\ge 1\).
examples.solution:
At n=1 both sides equal 5. Assume the identity for \(k\ge 1\). Adding the new term gives

\[\frac{k(k+1)(4k+11)}6+(k+1)(2k+5)=\frac{(k+1)(k+2)(4k+15)}6.\]

Since 4k+15=4(k+1)+11, this is exactly the k+1 formula. With the base case, induction proves the stated identity for every integer \(n\ge 1\).

examples.title: 3 · A bound needs its own algebraic bridge
examples.question: Prove \(3^n\ge n^2\) for every integer \(n\ge 2\).
examples.solution:
At n=2, \(9\ge 4\). Assume \(3^{k}\ge k^{2}\) for \(k\ge 2\). Multiplication by 3 preserves the inequality. Also

\[3k^2-(k+1)^2=2(k-2)^2+6(k-2)+3\ge3>0.\]

Thus \(3^{k+1}\ge 3k^{2}\ge (k+1)^{2}\). The base and implication establish the bound for all integers \(n\ge 2\). Merely replacing k by k+1 in the assumption would not prove this step.

examples.title: 4 · Three matches can still conceal a false formula
examples.question: A proposed formula for \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}(2r-1)\) is \(n^2+(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)\). Find the first failure, then prove the correct formula.
examples.solution:
The extra factor vanishes at 1, 2 and 3. At n=4 the actual sum is 16, but the proposal gives 22. The correct statement is \(S_{n}=n^{2}\). Its base n=1 gives 1=1. Assuming \(S_{k}=k^{2}\),

\[S_{k+1}=k^2+2k+1=(k+1)^2.\]

Hence \(S_{n}=n^{2}\) for every integer \(n\ge 1\) by induction. The counterexample rejects the proposal; the separate induction establishes its replacement.

lessons.title: Induction through repeated differentiation
lessons.summary: Track the derivative order, signs and factorials through an explicit next step.
lessons.objective: Prove derivative formulae with the correct order increment and domain.
lessons.before: Complete the induction framework. Review the product and chain rules, factorials, and derivatives of exponential, rational and trigonometric functions.
lessons.ideas:
The index counts an operation

Write \(D^n y=d^ny/dx^n\). For an ordinary nth-derivative formula, differentiate the assumed kth formula once. Keep n fixed while differentiating in x: factorials and powers depending only on k are constants.

You may start at n=0 if \(D^{0}y\) means y itself and the proposed formula is defined there. A formula involving (n−1)! usually starts at 1; do not invent (−1)! to force an earlier base.

An even-order statement moves by two derivatives

If P(n) describes \(D^{2n}y\), then P(k+1) describes \(D^{2k+2}y\). Differentiate the assumed formula twice. A one-derivative step reaches an odd order instead. For a formula repeating every four derivatives, use four derivatives per step.

Show the coefficient update

A claimed formula is not justified by spotting the first few derivatives. Use the chain rule, signs and factorial relation explicitly; for example \((k+1)k!=(k+1)!\). For a product of a polynomial and an exponential, differentiate both factors and collect the result into the exact proposed next polynomial.

Retain the x-domain where the original function and all required derivatives exist. State both quantifiers: every allowed derivative index and every x in that domain.
lessons.method:
1. Define the derivative-order statement and domain.
  2. Check the starting derivative directly.
  3. Assume the exact kth formula.
  4. Differentiate the number of times that advances the index once.
  5. Collect coefficients into the k+1 formula and conclude.
mistakes: An index increment is not always one differentiation.
The sign from differentiating a reciprocal must be retained.
Treat k as a constant when differentiating in x.
Check that the factorial is defined at the base case.

examples.title: 1 · A one-derivative bridge
examples.question: Prove \(D^n(e^{5x-1})=5^ne^{5x-1}\) for every integer \(n\ge 0\) and real x.
examples.solution:
For n=0 the identity is the original function. Assume the kth formula. Differentiating once, with \(5^{k}\) constant, gives

\[D^{k+1}(e^{5x-1})=5^k\cdot5e^{5x-1}=5^{k+1}e^{5x-1}.\]

Therefore the identity holds for all integers \(n\ge 0\) and all real x by induction.

examples.title: 2 · A factorial and a chain-rule factor
examples.question: For x>2/3 prove \(D^n(3x-2)^{-1}=(-1)^n n!3^n(3x-2)^{-n-1}\), \(n\ge 0\).
examples.solution:
At n=0 the expression is the original function. Suppose the formula holds for k. Differentiate the x-dependent factor:

\[D^{k+1}y=(-1)^kk!3^k(-k-1)3(3x-2)^{-k-2}=(-1)^{k+1}(k+1)!3^{k+1}(3x-2)^{-(k+1)-1}.\]

This is the required next formula, so induction proves the result for all \(n\ge 0\) on x>2/3. The excluded pole is never reintroduced.

examples.title: 3 · Four differentiations advance one index
examples.question: Let \(y=e^x\cos x\). Prove \(D^{4n}y=(-4)^ny\), \(n\ge 0\).
examples.solution:
Direct differentiation gives \(y'=e^{x}(cos\) x−sin x), \(y''=-2e^{x}sin\) x, \(y'''=-2e^{x}(sin\) x+cos x), and \(y^{(4)}=-4y\). P(0) is y=y. If \(D^{4k}y=(-4)^{k}y\), differentiating four times gives

\[D^{4k+4}y=(-4)^kD^4y=(-4)^{k+1}y.\]

The base and implication establish the formula for every integer \(n\ge 0\). Differentiating only once would not reach P(k+1).

examples.title: 4 · Use both terms of the product rule
examples.question: For \(y=(x-2)e^{2x}\), prove \(D^ny=2^ne^{2x}(x-2+n/2)\), \(n\ge 0\).
examples.solution:
The n=0 case is immediate. Assume the kth expression. Differentiating both factors gives

\[D^{k+1}y=2^ke^{2x}\bigl(2(x-2+k/2)+1\bigr)=2^{k+1}e^{2x}\bigl(x-2+(k+1)/2\bigr).\]

This reaches the exact next formula. Hence it is valid for every integer \(n\ge 0\) and real x.

lessons.title: Recursive formulae and invariant bounds
lessons.summary: Use the recurrence to carry a formula or an interval forward, with enough initial cases.
lessons.objective: Prove explicit sequence formulae and bounds without assuming a denominator sign or a missing initial case.
lessons.before: Review the forward implication, inequalities and recurrence notation. An invariant interval is an interval the recurrence maps back into itself.
lessons.ideas:
The recurrence supplies the implication

For \(u_{n+1}=g(u_n,n)\), substitute the induction hypothesis into g and simplify. Verify the actual first index, which may be 0. An explicit formula guessed from numerical terms still needs this argument.

A second-order recurrence needs two starting values

If \(u_{n+2}=a u_{n+1}+b u_n\), prove the proposed formula at both 0 and 1. Assume it at k and k+1, then derive it at k+2. Equivalently, induct on the paired statement that both consecutive cases hold. One initial check cannot determine a two-initial-value sequence.

Bounds must survive the actual map

To prove \(L<u_n<U\), first check the starting value. Assuming both inequalities at k, establish that the next term is defined, then show both new inequalities. In a rational recurrence the denominator's positivity must follow from the assumed interval before an inequality is multiplied through it.

For a square-root recurrence, check the radicand and the non-negative branch before squaring a proposed bound. A bounded sequence need not converge; a monotone bounded sequence does. If a limit is requested, justify convergence first, then use continuity of the recurrence on its interval and select an admissible fixed point.
lessons.method:
1. Record the starting index and all initial values.
  2. State a formula or invariant interval precisely.
  3. Check the needed base cases.
  4. Apply the recurrence to the assumed case(s), justifying domains and signs.
  5. Conclude induction; prove monotonicity separately if a limit is needed.
mistakes: One base case is insufficient for a general second-order recurrence.
Do not reverse the implication by assuming the next formula.
A denominator may change the direction of an inequality.
Boundedness alone does not justify taking a limit.

examples.title: 1 · An affine recurrence with index 0
examples.question: If \(u_{0}=4\) and \(u_{n+1}=2u_n+3\), prove \(u_n=7\cdot2^n-3\), \(n\ge 0\).
examples.solution:
At n=0, \(7-3=4=u_{0}\). Assume \(u_{k}=7\cdot 2^{k}-3\). The recurrence gives

\[u_{k+1}=2(7\cdot2^k-3)+3=7\cdot2^{k+1}-3.\]

Thus the formula holds for all integers \(n\ge 0\) by induction. Starting at 1 would have left the supplied first term outside the conclusion.

examples.title: 2 · Prove a denominator sign before using a bound
examples.question: Let \(v_{0}=1/2\) and \(v_{n+1}=(2v_n+3)/(v_n+4)\). Prove 0<\(v_{n}\)<1 for all \(n\ge 0\).
examples.solution:
The base lies in (0,1). Suppose 0<\(v_{k}\)<1. Then \(v_{k}+4\)>0 and \(2v_{k}+3\)>0, so \(v_{k+1}\)>0. Also

\[1-v_{k+1}=\frac{1-v_k}{v_k+4}>0.\]

Both next inequalities hold and the next term is defined. By induction all terms belong to (0,1); neither endpoint is attained.

examples.title: 3 · Carry two consecutive cases
examples.question: Given \(w_{0}=1\), \(w_{1}=4\) and \(w_{n+2}=4w_{n+1}-3w_n\), prove \(w_n=(3^{n+1}-1)/2\).
examples.solution:
The formula gives 1 at n=0 and 4 at n=1. Assume it holds at k and k+1. Then

\[w_{k+2}=\frac{4(3^{k+2}-1)-3(3^{k+1}-1)}2=\frac{3^{k+3}-1}2.\]

This proves the next case while retaining the k+1 case. Induction on the pair of consecutive statements establishes the formula for all \(n\ge 0\).

examples.title: 4 · A square-root map preserves an interval
examples.question: If \(u_{0}=2\) and \(u_{n+1}=\sqrt{6+u_n}\), prove \(2\le u_{n}\)<3 for all \(n\ge 0\).
examples.solution:
The base satisfies both bounds. Suppose \(2\le u_{k}\)<3. Then \(8\le 6+u_{k}\)<9. The radicand is positive, and the non-negative square-root function is increasing, so

\[2<\sqrt8\le u_{k+1}<3.\]

In particular \(2\le u_{k+1}\)<3. Induction proves the claimed interval for every \(n\ge 0\); strictness of the upper bound is preserved.

lessons.title: Induction for matrix powers
lessons.summary: Multiply the assumed matrix formula in the correct order and verify every entry.
lessons.objective: Prove matrix-power identities, including parity patterns and nilpotent corrections.
lessons.before: Review matrix multiplication and the induction framework. Use the identity matrix I, with \(A^{0}=I\) for any square A.
lessons.ideas:
An entrywise claim about a whole matrix

To prove \(A^{n}=F(n)\), check every entry at the base. Assuming \(A^{k}=F(k)\), calculate \(A^{k+1}=F(k)A\). It is also valid to multiply A on the left, but write the resulting order consistently. General matrices do not commute; identities for \((AB)^{n}\) require their own justification.

Use a small algebraic structure

If \(N^{2}=0\), multiplication shows \((I+cN)^n=I+ncN\). The proof uses \(N^{2}=0\) at the transition; checking a few powers only suggests the formula. If \(N^{3}=0\), a second correction survives:

\[(I+N)^n=I+nN+\frac{n(n-1)}2N^2.\]

Multiplying by I+N updates the \(N^{2}\) coefficient from k(k−1)/2 to k(k+1)/2, while the \(N^{3}\) term vanishes. Establish the nilpotent identity for the actual matrix first.

Parity and special parameter values

When \(A^{2}=cI\), prove the even and odd powers together: \(A^{2n}=c^nI\) and \(A^{2n+1}=c^nA\). A step in n multiplies by \(A^{2}\). Do not use an even-only base and then conclude every exponent has the even formula. Parameter-dependent formulae must remain defined at exceptional values; check those separately if your derivation divides by a parameter.
lessons.method:
1. Specify \(n\ge 0\) or the true starting exponent.
  2. Check the identity matrix or first power entry by entry.
  3. Assume the complete matrix formula.
  4. Multiply in the stated order and simplify every entry.
  5. Identify the exact next formula and conclude on its stated domain.
mistakes: \(A^{0}\) is the identity matrix, not the zero matrix.
Do not replace matrix multiplication with entrywise multiplication.
An even-power formula does not automatically cover odd powers.
A proof for a generic parameter must not discard a zero-parameter case.

examples.title: 1 · A non-triangular matrix with a simple correction
examples.question: For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}3&-2\\2&-1\end{pmatrix}\), prove \(A^n=I+2nN\), where \(N=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}\), \(n\ge 0\).
examples.solution:
Direct multiplication gives \(N^{2}=0\) and A=I+2N. The base n=0 is \(A^{0}=I\). Assuming \(A^{k}=I+2kN\),

\[A^{k+1}=(I+2kN)(I+2N)=I+2(k+1)N+4kN^2=I+2(k+1)N.\]

Thus the complete matrix identity holds for every \(n\ge 0\) by induction, even though A itself is not triangular.

examples.title: 2 · Opposite signs on a diagonal
examples.question: Prove \(\operatorname{diag}(2,-3)^n=\operatorname{diag}(2^n,(-3)^n)\), \(n\ge 0\).
examples.solution: At n=0 both matrices are I. Assume the kth formula. Multiplying by diag(2,−3) multiplies the first diagonal entry by 2 and the second by −3; both off-diagonal entries remain zero. The result is \(diag(2^{k+1}\),\((-3)^{k+1})\), proving P(k+1). Hence induction establishes all non-negative powers, including the alternating sign.

examples.title: 3 · Prove both parity cases
examples.question: For \(C=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\), prove \(C^{2n}=I\) and \(C^{2n+1}=C\) for \(n\ge 0\).
examples.solution: Compute \(C^{2}=I\). At n=0 the paired claims are \(C^{0}=I\) and \(C^{1}=C\). Assume both claims for k. Multiplying each by \(C^{2}=I\) yields \(C^{2k+2}=I\) and \(C^{2k+3}=C\). These are exactly the pair at k+1. Therefore both claims hold for all \(n\ge 0\) by induction.

examples.title: 4 · A quadratic correction in a 3 by 3 matrix
examples.question: Let \(J=\begin{pmatrix}0&2&0\\0&0&1\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}\). Prove \((I+J)^n=I+nJ+n(n-1)J^2/2\), \(n\ge 0\).
examples.solution:
\(J^{2}\) has only its top-right entry non-zero, equal to 2, and \(J^{3}=0\). The formula is I at n=0. Assuming it for k, multiplication by I+J gives

\[I+(k+1)J+\left(k+\frac{k(k-1)}2\right)J^2=I+(k+1)J+\frac{k(k+1)}2J^2.\]

The discarded term is a multiple of \(J^{3}=0\). This proves the k+1 formula and completes induction for all \(n\ge 0\).

lessons.title: Divisibility and a complete inductive argument
lessons.summary: Carry an integer multiple or a residue forward, and conclude on the correct index set.
lessons.objective: Prove divisibility statements by an explicit integer bridge and handle restricted indices precisely.
lessons.before: Complete the induction framework. Review factors, integer multiples, residues and products of consecutive integers.
lessons.ideas:
Keep the integer witness visible

To prove d divides f(n), with a fixed non-zero integer d, assume f(k)=dq for an integer q. Try to express

\[f(k+1)=a f(k)+dR(k),\]

where a is an integer and R(k) is an integer for every admissible k. The next value is then d(aq+R(k)), an integer multiple of d. The base case must also be divisible by d. Simply saying that an expression looks even or divisible does not establish an integer witness.

Two useful transitions

For polynomial f, factor the difference f(k+1)−f(k). For exponential f, a multiple a f(k) may cancel a difficult exponential term. If a remaining product needs an extra factor, justify it: consecutive integers have an even product, and a residue check may establish a factor of 3.

Congruences state the same integer fact

The statement f(n)≡r(n) (mod d) means d divides f(n)−r(n). It may be easier to prove this stronger residue statement first, then identify every n for which the residue is zero. A statement for odd indices requires an odd-index transition, or a re-indexed variable; do not silently conclude it for even integers too.

For a complete proof, record the allowed starting integer, use the hypothesis explicitly, justify the remaining integer multiple, and give the exact final domain. Short checks below practise those ingredients; a correct fragment is not certification of a complete written proof.
lessons.method:
1. State the divisor, function and integer domain.
  2. Check the actual first case.
  3. Write the hypothesis as an integer multiple or congruence.
  4. Produce a transition with an explicitly divisible remainder.
  5. Conclude with the base, implication and precise set of indices.
mistakes: A rational quotient is not necessarily an integer.
Changing a residue without justification can invalidate the step.
For an odd-index claim the next admissible index is k+2.
A valid transition cannot replace a missing base case.

examples.title: 1 · Use a multiple of the previous expression
examples.question: Prove 4 divides \(5^{n}-1\) for every integer \(n\ge 0\).
examples.solution:
At n=0 the expression is 0, a multiple of 4. Assume \(5^{k}-1=4q\) with integer q. Then

\[5^{k+1}-1=5(5^k-1)+4=4(5q+1).\]

The bracket is an integer, proving the next case. By induction the claim holds for every integer \(n\ge 0\).

examples.title: 2 · Factor a polynomial difference
examples.question: Prove 6 divides (n+1)(n+2)(n+3) for every integer \(n\ge 0\).
examples.solution:
For n=0 the product is 6. Put f(n)=(n+1)(n+2)(n+3) and assume f(k)=6q. Then

\[f(k+1)-f(k)=3(k+2)(k+3).\]

One of k+2 and k+3 is even, so (k+2)(k+3)/2 is an integer. Thus f(k+1)=6(q+(k+2)(k+3)/2), an integer multiple of 6. The base and implication prove the result for all \(n\ge 0\).

examples.title: 3 · Match one of two exponential growth factors
examples.question: Prove 7 divides \(9^{n}+6\cdot 2^{n}\) for all integers \(n\ge 0\).
examples.solution:
The n=0 value is 7. Put \(f(n)=9^{n}+6\cdot 2^{n}\) and assume f(k)=7q. Then

\[f(k+1)=2f(k)+7\cdot9^k=7(2q+9^k).\]

Because q and \(9^{k}\) are integers, this establishes P(k+1). The base and implication prove divisibility by 7 for every \(n\ge 0\).

examples.title: 4 · An odd-index conclusion uses a step of two
examples.question: Prove 8 divides \(n^{2}-1\) for every positive odd integer n.
examples.solution:
The base n=1 gives 0. Assume k is a positive odd integer and \(k^{2}-1=8q\). The next odd integer is k+2, and

\[(k+2)^2-1=(k^2-1)+4(k+1)=8\left(q+\frac{k+1}2\right).\]

Since k is odd, (k+1)/2 is an integer. The base and step of two cover every positive odd integer. The conclusion does not include even integers: n=2 gives 3.

questions.title: An offset quadratic summand
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(S_{n}\) denote the sum below.

  1. Prove by mathematical induction, for every integer \(n\ge 1\),

    \[\sum_{r=1}^{n}r \left(r + 2\right)=\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 7\right)}{6}\][5]

  2. Hence evaluate \(\sum_{r=4}^{15}r(r+2)\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let P(n) be the stated identity. At n=1 both sides equal 3. Assume P(k) for an arbitrary integer \(k\ge 1\). Adding the new term gives

\[S_{k+1}=\frac{k \left(k + 1\right) \left(2 k + 7\right)}{6}+\left(k + 1\right) \left(k + 3\right)=\frac{\left(k + 1\right) \left(k + 2\right) \left(2 k + 9\right)}{6}\]

The last expression is F(k+1), with F the proposed right side. Thus P(k) implies P(k+1). The base case and implication establish the identity for all integers \(n\ge 1\).

(b)

Subtract \(S_{3}\) from \(S_{15}\): 1480−26=1454.
questions.hint_html: Add the term with r=k+1 to the assumed kth sum. A tail sum is the difference of two complete sums.

questions.title: When a running total first crosses a threshold
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(S_{n}\) denote the sum below.

  1. Prove by mathematical induction, for every integer \(n\ge 1\),

    \[\sum_{r=1}^{n}4 r - 1=n \left(2 n + 1\right)\][5]

  2. Find the least positive integer n for which the sum exceeds 400.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let P(n) be the stated identity. At n=1 both sides equal 3. Assume P(k) for an arbitrary integer \(k\ge 1\). Adding the new term gives

\[S_{k+1}=k \left(2 k + 1\right)+4 k + 3=\left(k + 1\right) \left(2 k + 3\right)\]

The last expression is F(k+1), with F the proposed right side. Thus P(k) implies P(k+1). The base case and implication establish the identity for all integers \(n\ge 1\).

(b)

\(S_{13}=351\) and \(S_{14}=406\). Every added term 4r−1 is positive, so the least index is 14.

questions.title: A finite reciprocal sum and its remainder
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(S_{n}\) denote the sum below.

  1. Prove by mathematical induction, for every integer \(n\ge 1\),

    \[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\left(r + 1\right) \left(r + 2\right)}=\frac{n}{2 n + 4}\][5]

  2. Find the least \(n\ge 1\) for which \(1/2-S_n<1/50\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let P(n) be the stated identity. At n=1 both sides equal \frac{1}{6}. Assume P(k) for an arbitrary integer \(k\ge 1\). Adding the new term gives

\[S_{k+1}=\frac{k}{2 k + 4}+\frac{1}{\left(k + 2\right) \left(k + 3\right)}=\frac{k + 1}{2 \left(k + 3\right)}\]

The last expression is F(k+1), with F the proposed right side. Thus P(k) implies P(k+1). The base case and implication establish the identity for all integers \(n\ge 1\).

(b)

The remainder is 1/(n+2). The strict inequality gives n+2>50, so \(n\ge 49\) and the least value is 49.

questions.title: Cubes along an odd-index progression
